items.question: Trace the evolution of India's science and technology policy from the Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958 to the draft STIP 2020, highlighting the shift in emphasis over time.
items.modelAnswer: India's science policy has evolved from **building basic scientific capacity** to **innovation-led, self-reliant growth**. The **Scientific Policy Resolution (SPR) 1958**, under Nehru, sought to **cultivate science and the scientific temper** and secure for the people the benefits of science, laying the base for institutions like CSIR, DAE and later DST (1971). The **Technology Policy Statement (TPS) 1983**, in the Indira Gandhi era, shifted focus to **technological self-reliance** and indigenous capability, reducing import dependence. The **Science and Technology Policy (STP) 2003** integrated science with technology, called for **higher investment (aiming at 2% of GDP)** and linked S&T to equity and national development. The **Science, Technology and Innovation Policy (STIP) 2013** was a landmark — it introduced **'Innovation'** into the title, adopted the theme **'STI for the People,'** and aspired to place India **among the top five global scientific powers** while reiterating the **2% GERD** goal. The **draft STIP 2020**, prepared by the **Office of the PSA and DST** through a **decentralised, bottom-up consultative process**, envisions self-reliance, inclusivity and an open-science ecosystem — but remains **un-notified as of 2026**. The trajectory thus moves from **knowledge-building (1958) -> self-reliance (1983) -> integration & investment (2003) -> innovation & global standing (2013) -> inclusive, decentralised STI (2020)**. Yet a persistent gap remains: **actual R&D spend is about 0.64% of GDP**, far below the repeated 2% aspiration, underscoring that policy intent has outpaced financing. Recent structural reforms — the **ANRF (2023)** and the **RDI Scheme (2025)** — attempt to close this by mobilising private funding.
keyPoints: SPR 1958 (Nehru): cultivate science and scientific temper; benefits for the people.
TPS 1983 (Indira Gandhi): technological self-reliance and indigenous capability.
STP 2003 (Vajpayee): integrate S&T, raise investment toward 2% GDP, link to equity.
STIP 2013: 'Innovation' added; 'STI for the People'; top-5 scientific power; 2% GERD goal.
Draft STIP 2020 (PSA + DST): decentralised, bottom-up, inclusive; not yet notified.
Recurring gap: real GERD about 0.64% of GDP; ANRF 2023 and RDI Scheme 2025 seek to raise private R&D.
items.source: DST — evolution of S&T policy; draft STIP 2020; PIB

items.question: "India's research and development ecosystem suffers from chronic under-investment." Examine this statement and discuss how recent institutional reforms seek to address it.
items.modelAnswer: India's R&D ecosystem is **structurally under-funded**. Its **Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) is about 0.64% of GDP** — far below the **2% target** repeated since 2003, and behind China (about 2.4%), the USA, Korea and Israel. Two structural weaknesses stand out: **(i)** the **government funds the bulk of R&D**, while the **private-sector contribution is unusually low** (the reverse of most innovation leaders), and **(ii)** research funding was **fragmented and grant-application heavy**, discouraging long-horizon and translational work. The consequences include limited deep-tech commercialisation and reliance on imported technology. **Recent reforms** target these gaps. The **Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) Act, 2023** creates an **apex funding body** (subsuming SERB) with an envisaged **Rs 50,000 crore over 2023-28**, of which **about Rs 36,000 crore is to come from industry and philanthropy** — explicitly **crowding in private funding** and aligning with NEP 2020; the **PM chairs its Governing Board**. The **RDI Scheme (2025)**, with a corpus of about **Rs 1 lakh crore**, offers **long-tenure, low-cost financing** to spur **private-sector R&D in sunrise and strategic sectors**. Mission-mode programmes — the **National Quantum Mission (Rs 6,003.65 cr)**, the **National Supercomputing Mission (PARAM)** and **NM-ICPS** — build deep-tech capacity, while **One Nation One Subscription (2025)** widens researchers' access to global journals. Together these signal a shift from **fragmented public grants** toward a **coordinated, private-leveraged, mission-driven** ecosystem. For sustained impact, India must also strengthen the **research-industry-university linkage**, retain talent, and steadily raise GERD toward the 2% goal.
keyPoints: India's GERD is about 0.64% of GDP, well short of the 2% target and behind China/USA/Korea.
Structural weaknesses: government funds most R&D; private-sector share is low; funding was fragmented.
ANRF Act 2023 (Rs 50,000 cr, ~Rs 36,000 cr from private sources; PM-chaired) is the apex funding reform.
RDI Scheme 2025 (about Rs 1 lakh crore) provides low-cost finance for private-sector R&D.
Missions (Quantum, Supercomputing, NM-ICPS) and ONOS build deep-tech capacity and access.
Way forward: stronger industry-academia links, talent retention, and raising GERD toward 2%.
items.source: DST R&D Statistics; ANRF Act 2023; PIB — RDI Scheme, National Quantum Mission

items.question: What is meant by 'scientific temper'? Discuss its constitutional basis and its relevance for governance and society in India.
items.modelAnswer: **Scientific temper** refers to a **rational, evidence-based and questioning attitude** — the disposition to accept claims on the basis of **observation, reason and experiment** rather than superstition, dogma or unverified belief. The term was popularised by **Jawaharlal Nehru** and finds explicit constitutional expression in **Article 51A(h)**, which makes it a **Fundamental Duty** of every citizen to develop the **scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform** — inserted by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976** on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. India is among the very few nations to constitutionally enshrine it, and it complements the **1958 Scientific Policy Resolution's** aim to cultivate science among the people. For **governance**, scientific temper underpins **evidence-based policymaking** — data-driven schemes, technology in service delivery (e.g., India Stack, DBT), and rational responses to public-health and disaster challenges (as seen during COVID-19). For **society**, it counters **misinformation, pseudoscience and harmful practices**, promotes **critical thinking and innovation**, and supports **inclusive development** by empowering citizens to make informed choices. Challenges persist — the spread of **fake news and deepfakes**, persistence of superstition, and uneven science education. Strengthening scientific temper therefore calls for **quality STEM education, public science communication, digital/media literacy** and institutions that reward inquiry — reinforcing the STI-for-the-People vision and India's ambitions as an innovation-driven economy.
keyPoints: Scientific temper = a rational, evidence-based, questioning attitude over superstition/dogma.
Constitutional basis: Article 51A(h), a Fundamental Duty added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Term popularised by Nehru; complements the 1958 Scientific Policy Resolution.
Governance relevance: evidence-based policy, tech-enabled delivery, rational crisis response.
Societal relevance: counters misinformation/pseudoscience, promotes critical thinking and innovation.
Way forward: STEM education, science communication and media/digital literacy.
items.source: Constitution of India Article 51A(h); 42nd Amendment 1976; SPR 1958
